content: Coronaviruses are a genus of animal viruses that belong to the family Coronaviridae. They are named for their crown-like surface projections, which were first observed when the virus was isolated from chickens in 1937. In 1965, Tyrell and Bynoe successfully propagated the first human coronavirus (HCoV) in vitro using cultures of human ciliated embryonal trachea. Currently, there are approximately 15 species within this family, which can infect not only humans but also cattle, pigs, rodents, cats, dogs, and birds. Some of these viruses are significant veterinary pathogens, particularly in chickens. Coronaviruses gained global attention during the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) epidemic caused by SARS-CoV in 2002–2003. Another novel coronavirus, MERS-CoV, emerged in 2012, causing the Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS) epidemic. In 2019, a new coronavirus, 2019-nCoV, was identified as the cause of a respiratory illness outbreak in Wuhan, China. Coronaviruses can be classified into three groups based on their genetic and replication characteristics. They can also be categorized by their ability to infect humans. These infections are widespread globally and are responsible for 10–15% of common cold cases. The incidence of infection is strongly seasonal, with the highest rates occurring in children during winter months. Adult infections are less common. The exact number of coronavirus serotypes and the extent of antigenic variation remain unknown. Reinfections throughout life suggest the presence of multiple serotypes (at least four are known) and/or antigenic variation, which complicates the development of effective immunization strategies. The exact incidence rate of coronavirus infections is difficult to estimate due to limited data. The case fatality rate of 2019-nCoV in the first 99 patients at a Wuhan hospital was reported to be 11%. The most significant risk factor for coronavirus infection is exposure to infected animals or humans. Routine screening for coronavirus infection is not currently recommended due to insufficient evidence. The clinical course of coronavirus infection can vary widely, ranging from subclinical cases to overt clinical conditions. Respiratory distress is the most common complication, often necessitating mechanical ventilation and intensive care unit (ICU) management. Prognosis depends on the specific virus type and disease presentation. Young children, the elderly, immunocompromised individuals, and those with comorbid conditions are at the highest risk for poor outcomes. Diagnosis of human coronavirus infections relies on a combination of clinical and epidemiological criteria. Close contact with infected individuals, travel to endemic areas, and detection of viral RNA in the patient’s serum are critical for confirming the diagnosis. The history of exposure to infected animals or humans is also important. Patients typically report flu-like symptoms in the early stages, which may progress to upper respiratory symptoms. Common symptoms include fever, cough, and shortness of breath. The incubation period varies depending on the specific infection. Physical examination findings in coronavirus-infected patients often include fever, flu-like symptoms, cough, and body aches. The general appearance of the patient depends on the incubation period of the illness. Chest X-ray findings in suspected cases may resemble those seen in pneumonia. Electrocardiogram (ECG) findings are nonspecific but may include sinus tachycardia and diffuse T-wave inversion. Chest CT scans may reveal unilateral or bilateral pneumonia, mottling, ground-glass opacities, focal or multifocal opacities, consolidation, and septal thickening, with subpleural and lower lobe involvement being more common. MRI findings are not specific to coronavirus infections but may assist in diagnosis by exclusion. Laboratory tests, including serology for viral antigens, molecular testing, and viral culture, can confirm coronavirus infection. However, these tests are not commonly used due to the typically mild nature of the illness and the limited availability of specialized laboratories. Research laboratories have employed methods such as isolation, electron microscopy, serology, and PCR-based assays for surveillance studies. Treatment for coronavirus infections is primarily supportive, as no specific antiviral therapy is currently available. Most individuals with coronavirus illness recover on their own without the need for specialized treatment.
